items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

items.summary: React Native lets you build real mobile apps for Android and iOS using JavaScript and React. Instead of learning two separate languages and maintaining two codebases, you write one app and it runs on both platforms. That is why startups and small teams love it: one team, one codebase, two app stores. If you already know JavaScript, React Native is the shortest path to publishing a mobile app. How does React Native work? You build your app from components, just like a React website — but instead of HTML elements, you use native components like View, Text, and TouchableOpacity, which render as real native controls on the phone. JavaScript handles the logic, and a bridge talks to the phone's native features: camera, GPS, notifications. You write the code once, and the same logic runs on both Android and iOS, with small platform-specific tweaks where needed. React Native is a good fit for beginners who already know JavaScript and React because almost everything transfers: components, state, props, hooks. items.summary: I needed to submit 174 URLs to Google's Indexing API from a production server running Python 3.8 with system pip. The official quickstart uses google-auth, which meant either polluting system packages or spinning up a venv just to run one script. So I did it with Node's built-in crypto instead. items.title: How to Choose an Affordable Logging API for Small Projects — 3 Node.js Checkout Signals
items.summary: TL;DR: For a small logistics project, choose a logging API by the failure signal it preserves per retained byte. Start with structured checkout events, keep a short searchable window, and send only a sampled or aggregated residue to long-term storage. The least complex design is one request-scoped record for each checkout attempt, plus a full error record when the attempt fails. A useful budget starts with arithmetic, not a vendor comparison. Imagine 10,000 checkout attempts per day and one 1.5 KB structured event per attempt. Thirty days of raw retention is about 450 MB before indexes, metadata, retries, and replication. If the application emits five near-duplicate lines per attempt, that same event stream becomes roughly 2.25 GB. The dominant term is the volume retained, so a lower ingest price cannot rescue an unbounded retention policy. The example is deliberately small. It gives a team a number it can inspect, change, and challenge. It also exposes the real choice: preserve enough context to reconstruct a failed delivery checkout, while refusing to keep every successful state transition forever. items.summary: Un formulario moderno no solo debe enviar datos. También tiene que explicar qué está ocurriendo mientras el usuario escribe, valida, espera una respuesta o corrige un error. Cuando esos estados no están bien diseñados, la interfaz parece lenta aunque la red responda en pocos milisegundos. En proyectos React he encontrado que una mejora pequeña, como reservar espacio para un mensaje de error o devolver el foco al campo correcto, suele tener más impacto que añadir otra librería. La idea es tratar el formulario como una secuencia de estados visibles y medibles, no como un botón con un spinner. Un campo de email puede pasar por varios estados distintos: vacío y listo para recibir entrada; escribiendo, con una validación que todavía no terminó; válido, pero esperando el envío; rechazado, con una explicación que se puede corregir; enviado, con una confirmación que no desaparece demasiado rápido. El problema típico es representar todos esos casos con un único isLoading. items.title: A PDF Writer in 40 Lines: Turning Photos Into PDFs in the Browser, No Library
items.summary: We are a small Saudi team in Riyadh, and one of our 200 free browser tools turns photos into a PDF. People use it for receipts, ID scans, homework and contracts, so two things mattered: the photos must never be uploaded, and the page must stay light on a phone. The usual answer is to load a PDF library. We didn't. The whole writer is about 40 lines of plain JavaScript, and in our test its output passed a strict parser and opened in MuPDF without any repair. This post walks through how it works and the five small traps we hit. A PDF page can hold an image object with /Filter /DCTDecode. That filter is JPEG. So if you already have JPEG bytes, you can drop them into the file unchanged: no decoding, no compression code, no library. And the browser gives you JPEG bytes for free: const blob = await new Promise(r => canvas.toBlob(r, "image/jpeg", 0.8)); const jpeg = new Uint8Array(await blob.arrayBuffer()); Everything else is just writing a few text objects around those bytes. items.title: 401 vs 403 in your Node API logs: what each pattern means
items.summary: A 401 and a 403 sit next to each other in the log, both amber and both "auth stuff". They answer different questions, though, and the pattern each one makes over an hour tells you whether you're looking at an attack, a scraper or your own deploy. RFC 9110 section 15.5.2 defines 401 Unauthorized as a request that "lacks valid authentication credentials for the target resource." The server sending it must include a WWW-Authenticate header with at least one challenge. The challenge in that header tells the client how to authenticate. Section 15.5.4 defines 403 Forbidden: the server understood the request and refuses it. If credentials came with the request, they aren't enough, and the client should not retry with the same ones. The server knows who you are and the answer is still no. So 401 is about identity and 403 is about permission. If your API keeps them apart, the four patterns below are easy to pick out of a log. Dozens of failed logins in a few seconds followed by one success is a password or key that worked. The 401s alone are noise you see every day. The 200 after them is the line to alert on. We covered the wider version of this in spotting credential stuffing. /invoices/10

items.title: Node.js Realtime Logout in 2026 — Token Revocation and Forced Disconnect
items.summary: TL;DR: Treat logout as two separate controls. Revoke the credential so the next authorization fails, then disconnect the authenticated identity so its current socket stops receiving fan-out. Finally, check channel presence; a successful revoke response alone does not prove that a live client is gone. For a B2B SaaS session that combines a live poll with a support chat widget, I would make that sequence the server-side logout contract. The invariant is blunt: after logout completes, the old token cannot authorize again and the old identity is absent from the channels whose data it must no longer receive. This matters more than which Node.js WebSocket wrapper happens to be open in the browser. Infrai fits the server-side control portion of that architecture when the team wants revoke, disconnect, and verification behind the same REST contract used for adjacent backend capabilities. It doesn't remove the need to own the logout invariant. Revocation affects the next authorization, not the socket that has already passed authorization. items.title: Handoff: Trustless Escrow for the Digital Economy
items.summary: The digital creator economy is built on "trust me bro." When you buy an API key, a piece of code, or a digital account from someone online, one person has to go first. If the buyer pays first, the seller can ghost them. If the seller delivers first, the buyer can take the files and run. Handoff is a trustless escrow protocol on Solana that fixes this. What it does The Buyer locks USDC in a smart contract. The Seller accepts the deal and delivers the digital asset. The Buyer gets a time-locked window to inspect the asset. If they approve, the funds instantly release to the Seller. If the seller ghosts, the buyer gets a refund. If the asset is fake, the funds freeze for a dispute. Why Solana? Speed & Cost: Transactions settle in milliseconds for fractions of a cent, making $50 trades viable. On-chain Escrow State Machine: The smart contract enforces the entire lifecycle: Initialized -> Accepted -> Delivered -> Completed/Disputed. The Tech Stack Smart Contract: Anchor (Rust). Frontend: React, Vite, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. Wallet: Phantom Wallet Adapter. items.summary: React 20 Compiler: Which Hooks It Eliminates, Which It Cannot, and How to Audit Your Codebase Before Upgrading This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review. The React Compiler shipped with React 19 as a stable Babel plugin that automatically memoizes components and hooks, eliminating the majority of manual useMemo, useCallback, and React.memo calls. Teams installing version 1.0.0 today find that most performance-oriented memoization becomes redundant. The compiler analyzes data flow, understands mutability, and applies granular memoization that survives conditional returns and early exits where manual hooks fail. The problem surfaces when developers treat the compiler as a drop-in replacement without auditing the semantic contracts their existing hooks enforce. A useCallback wrapping an event handler for performance looks identical in the source to one ensuring exact reference identity for a useEffect dependency array. The compiler sees both as memoization candidates, removes them, and breaks the second use case. items.title: Two emails about a new campaign, and whichever one goes first cancels the other for good
items.summary: A campaign in Nakodo is meant to be launched and then left alone, which how it works describes from the outside. The awkward part of that promise is the first hour. You press launch, a progress line starts moving, and then you close the tab, and whatever happens next has to reach you by email. Two things can happen next. Either the first good fits arrive, or a day passes and none do. So there are two emails, written by two functions in the same file, and most of the design is in making sure you never get both. The naive version sends as soon as there is one result. That is a worse email than it sounds: a campaign's first fit often arrives minutes after launch, while you are still looking at the screen that produced it, and an email telling you about one creator when thirty are coming is an email that trains you to ignore the next one. const ENOUGH_TO_EMAIL = 5; // good fits; fewer is still sent an hour after launch const WAIT_FOR_MORE_MS = 60 * 60 * 1000; const ready = rows.filter( (r) => r.email && (r.fit >= ENOUGH_TO_EMAIL || (r.launchedAt && Date.now() - r.launchedAt.getTime() > WAIT_FOR_MORE_MS)), ); A quorum with a timeout. items.title: A paid source ran out of credit and our own code hid it from us for nine days
items.summary: Nakodo leans on a handful of external sources, and two of them are paid, prepaid, and can therefore simply stop. On 12 October one of them ran out of balance. The work that depended on it stopped that day and did not start again for nine days. Nothing crashed, no alert fired, and the only record anywhere was a row in a counters table with a timestamp in it. Two separate mistakes made that possible, and they are worth separating, because only one of them is the obvious one. Every external source has a daily row, and a refusal from the source writes exhaustedAt on it. Every request first asks whether the row is usable: const usable = sql`${providerDays.exhaustedAt} is null`; That is correct for a source whose budget is a calendar day. A daily API quota resets at a fixed hour, so "it refused us, stop asking until the day turns over" is exactly right, and it saves a few thousand pointless requests. It is wrong for a prepaid balance, and wrong in a way that is almost funny. The day turns over. The first job of the new day asks the source. The source, still unpaid, refuses. items.title: Seven useMemo calls in 72,683 lines, six of them in one file, and the one that matters is not about speed
items.summary: Nakodo is a Next.js 16 app on React 19.2.8: 582 TypeScript files, 72,683 lines. Most advice about React performance is about memoisation, so I grepped the whole thing to see how much of it we actually use. useMemo 7 occurrences, 2 files useCallback 2 occurrences, 2 files React.memo / memo() 0 useDeferredValue 0 useLayoutEffect 0 useImperativeHandle 0 For scale, the same grep over the same tree finds useEffect in 23 files, useState in 33, useTransition in 11 and useActionState in 11. So the app is not short of client state. It is short of memoisation, and the reason turns out to be structural rather than principled. 226 of the files are .tsx. Eighty of them start with "use client", and 17 of those eighty are the shadcn primitives in src/components/ui. Everything else renders on the server, which includes almost every list in the product: the campaign list, the conversations screen, the creator page, all 76 public pages. A .map() over rows appears in 103 files, and in most of them it runs once, on a server, into HTML. React.memo protects a child from a parent that re-renders. items.summary: Open our FAQ page, open the console, and ask Chrome what is listening: const l = getEventListeners(document); console.log(Object.keys(l).length, "types,", Object.values(l).reduce((a, v) => a + v.length, 0), "listeners"); // 90 types, 152 listeners That page is prerendered HTML. items.title: Your inactive listing survived a successful upsert
items.summary: Your outreach queue still contains a listing that the latest exact-ID lookup marked inactive. The ingestion job finished. Your database is perfectly available. Somehow, that makes it more annoying. The quiet failure can sit inside your validator: it requires title, rejects the sparse status record, and leaves the previous listing eligible for outreach. An inactive tombstone must update outreach eligibility without replacing the last listing snapshot. A successful explicit lookup can produce that tombstone when the requested ID is absent. A failed lookup can't establish inactivity. A listing disappearing from a filtered search proves very little. Its price might have changed. It might no longer match your filters. An explicit lookup gives you a narrower observation: whether that lookup returned the requested advertisement. That distinction belongs in your database design before you schedule anything. Azure gives your App Service, Function App, container or VM an identity in Microsoft Entra ID. Your code asks for a token for that identity, and SQL Server accepts the token instead of a password. items.summary: Most abandoned carts are not a decision to leave. Someone got distracted, the page felt slow, or they meant to come back and forgot. A single reminder catches some of them. A sequence catches more, as long as it stops the moment the shopper buys. Here is how the cart recovery sequence in StoreFlux works, using the default timings. There are three emails. The defaults are 1 hour, 24 hours, and 72 hours (60, 1440, and 4320 minutes). The first is a gentle reminder, the second is a second nudge the next day, and the third is the one that can carry a recovery discount. Each stage's timing is configurable per store. Before each send, the sweeper checks whether the cart has converted to an order. If the shopper completed checkout, the remaining emails are not sent. Nobody gets a reminder about a purchase they already made. The third email can issue a recovery coupon, but only when two things are both true: the store has the include-coupon setting turned on, and the Coupons module is enabled for that tenant. items.title: Stop Copying a String Into a MemoryStream. .NET 11 Has StringStream
items.summary: TL;DR: .NET 11 adds StringStream, ReadOnlyMemoryStream, and WritableMemoryStream. They wrap a string, a ReadOnlyMemory , or a Memory as a Stream, so you stop copying data into a MemoryStream just to satisfy a method signature. This ships in .NET 11, which is at Release Candidate 2 with a go-live license, but is not GA yet. Everything below was run on the .NET 11 RC 1 SDK. Some API wants a Stream. You have a string. So you write the line that has been in every codebase since 2002: using var stream = new MemoryStream(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(text)); It works. It also encodes the entire string into a brand new byte[] before the parser reads a single byte. The same story repeats with buffers. You already have a ReadOnlyMemory from a pool, a socket, or a slice, and the only way to hand it to a Stream API was to call ToArray() and copy it, or write your own little wrapper class. Most teams have that wrapper somewhere, usually named MemoryStreamButBetter. Four new Stream types that sit directly on top of memory you already have: StringStream reads a string or ReadOnlyMemory as bytes in the encoding you pick. items.title: I Threw Away 786 MB of Scratch Buffers
items.summary: I had a message processor that unpacked each incoming record into a scratch buffer, read one value out, and moved on. The buffer was pure throwaway: fill it, peek at a byte, forget it. I wrote the obvious thing, new byte[4096] at the top of the loop, and shipped it. It worked. It was also quietly handing the garbage collector a short-lived 4 KB array every single iteration, and I didn't notice until I was staring at an allocation profile for something else and saw this loop sitting near the top. Here's the loop, more or less: for (int i = 0; i keeps a stash of reusable arrays. You Rent one when you need it and Return it when you're done, and the same physical arrays cycle through your loop instead of a fresh one each pass. for (int i = 0; i .Shared.Rent(bufferSize); try { Fill(scratch.AsSpan(0, bufferSize), i); sink += scratch[i % bufferSize]; } finally { ArrayPool .Shared.Return(scratch); } } Same loop, same result. The allocation line: ArrayPool : 0.0 MB allocated, 0 gen0 collections Zero. Once the pool warms up, the loop stops allocating entirely and the GC has nothing to collect. items.title: Breathe as One: a two-phone co-op game you win by breathing together
items.summary: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge Breathe as One is a little co-op game for two people and two iPhones. You win by breathing together. You sit across from each other with your phones propped up, front cameras facing you. Each phone only watches its own player. The SmartSpectra SDK picks up the rise and fall of your chest and turns it into a live wave, and the two phones swap those waves over a private nearby connection. So both screens show the same thing: your breath in blue and your partner's in coral. As you settle into the same rhythm, the two lines drift toward each other's color until they melt into one lilac line. Getting there is the whole game. A game takes a few minutes and has three rounds: Follow the Tide (45 s). A white wave rolls across the screen at 6 breaths a minute, and you both ride it. No Leader (60 s). The wave goes away and you have to find each other without a guide. It's harder than it sounds, and it's my favorite part. Heart Meet (45 s). items.title: I Summed 400,000 Rows on Every Refresh
items.summary: I had a little dashboard endpoint that summed a sales table by region. Nothing clever: filter the rows, add up the amounts, return a number. It felt instant in dev, so I stopped thinking about it. Then I left the page open on a second monitor. It auto-refreshes every few seconds, and when I tailed the logs I watched the same region total get recomputed over and over, each refresh redoing work whose answer hadn't moved since the last one. The underlying data changes maybe once an hour. I was aggregating 400,000 rows dozens of times a minute to produce a number I'd already produced. The usual reflex is to reach for IMemoryCache and wrap the computation. That works, but it caches inside the handler, so you still pay for model binding, the handler invocation, and serializing the result every single time. What I actually wanted was for the whole response to come back without my code running at all. That's what output caching does, and it's been sitting in ASP.NET Core since .NET 7. I'd just never turned it on. You register the services, add the middleware, and opt an endpoint in. Here's the shape of it: builder.Services.AddOutputCache(); // services var app = builder.Build(); app.UseOut

items.title: How to Stamp a Transparent PNG Logo Across a Batch of Photos in Swift
items.summary: If you need the same logo on thirty photos, the boring bugs show up immediately: the mark looks huge on a 12-megapixel still and timid on a 48-megapixel one, the PNG’s transparent background turns into a grey box, or the edges of the logo go muddy because the alpha channel was applied twice. This post walks through a small UIKit pipeline that loads a transparent PNG, draws each photo, then draws the logo at a size tied to the photo’s shorter side, inset by a percentage of the frame. I’m writing it from the seat of someone who builds BatchMark, an on-device batch photo app; the batch watermark path is where this idea lives in the product. The code below is a teaching extract, not a dump of the app. People say “put the logo in the corner” and mean three separate decisions: How large is it, visually? Not “200 pixels,” because 200 pixels is a different object on a 4032-pixel-wide photo than on a 8064-pixel-wide one. How far is it from the edges? A 40-point inset looks generous on a screenshot and lost on a full-resolution export. How does it sit on top of the photo? The PNG already has transparency. items.title: AlpineBSD Announced - an AI-free FOSS OS
items.summary: Lproven (Slashdot reader #6,030) shares his article about a new OS in the BSD family "combining NetBSD's kernel and libc with a port of the Alpine Linux userland" — and promising it won't use AI-generated code: AlpineBSD is so new that it barely exists yet. There are no installation media available, though it's possible to manually bootstrap an installation. What AlpineBSD does already have is an AI policy, and the plan is to avoid "the output of generative AI models (e.g. LLMs)" as far as possible: "Any software whose code, documentation, binaries, or other assets include, in any part, the output of a generative AI tool such as an LLM, is considered 'tainted' for our purposes...." Back in 2024, the NetBSD project made its position on AI plain. Its commit guidelines say that "code generated by a Large Language Model [...] is presumed to be tainted code...." AlpineBSD's ports repository and source code are hosted on Sourcehut, under the account of sircmpwn, better known as Drew DeVault... We will follow AlpineBSD with interest. items.title: Microsoft Removes PC-to-PC Migration from Windows 11, Points Users to OneDrive-Based Backup
items.summary: Windows 11 offered a PC-to-PC Migration feature that "moved files and settings directly between two PCs over Wi-Fi or Ethernet," reports Ghacks. But according to an updated Microsoft support page, the tool is no longer available. "Microsoft's support documentation now redirects users to Windows Backup, a tool that relies on OneDrive cloud storage instead of a direct connection between two computers..." Windows Backup works differently. It requires a personal Microsoft account and backs up supported folders (Desktop, Documents, Pictures, Videos and Music) to OneDrive. Free OneDrive accounts include only 5GB of storage, and Microsoft's own promotional screenshot for Windows Backup shows 4.5GB of that allowance already in use. Years of photos, documents and downloads can exceed the free tier quickly. Windows Backup does carry some extras. It can remember installed apps, Wi-Fi networks, passwords and some settings to speed up setup on a new device. Apps still have to be reinstalled, and supported files are restored from the cloud. Thanks to Slashdot reader joshuark for sharing the article. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Data Centers are Being Powered By Giant Gas Plants, Possibly Increasing Carbon Pollution for Decades
items.summary: Rather than racing toward their net-zero targets, Amazon and other AI/cloud computing companies "are driving emissions sharply higher," reports the Washington Post: To support their data centers, tech firms are driving construction of a new generation of supersized, gas-fired power plants that could lock in hundreds of millions of tons of climate pollution for decades to come, according to corporate disclosures and an analysis conducted for The Post by a researcher at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. Industry estimates show these projects have put the tech sector on course to grow from a modest driver of industrial carbon pollution into one of the world's biggest emitters of greenhouse gases. items.summary: In a SwiftUI reference app, streamed model output and illustrated answer cards repeatedly change the transcript’s height. The failure Opening “Ask guide” from an entry could leave the process hung at roughly 99% CPU. The sampled main thread repeatedly hit SwiftUI lazy-stack placement/graph updates, and the observed process footprint reached 1.1 GB. Reopening returned to the same hung process. A UI reproduction also timed out while querying the app. The transcript combined lazy height estimation, a scroll target on a growing answer, animated scrolling, and frequent streamed-text updates. Inspired by the events on industrial fridge installations in the past weeks, I wanted to see what people would try against a convincing fake. To learn more about this I built a honeypot that resembled perfectly the Danfoss AK-SM 800A and Dixell XWEB interfaces. Both of them are recognized on Shodan as real ones (an not as honeypots). It’s one Python file using only the standard library, and it builds on eppser/danfoss-ak-sm-decoy and public research by Synacktiv, Claroty and Ironhackers. Things that were fun to get right: - Matching real units. I used Shodan records of real devices to match header order, page titles, certificate fields and TLS versions. The Danfoss persona sends nginx headers in the same order as a real AK-SM 800A. The Dixell persona sends no Server header and pads its page to exactly 8,202 bytes. - Recognising exploit attempts. It recognises CVE-2025-41450, the Danfoss “code of the day” login bypass, and records whether the submitted code is correct for today. items.title: AlmaLinux Shows Advantages of ABI Compatibility After RHEL Restricted Source Code Access
items.summary: "AlmaLinux OS charted a new path in 2023 when Red Hat restricted source code access to Red Hat Enterprise Linux," remembers Linux Magazine. "Rather than pursue 1:1 compatibility with RHEL like other Enterprise Linux alternatives, the AlmaLinux OS Foundation chose application binary interface (ABI) compatibility, which guarantees that applications and kernel modules that work on RHEL will work on AlmaLinux OS." No longer constrained by the 1:1 promise, AlmaLinux can offer new features, or add back deprecated ones, while still remaining a stable, drop-in replacement for RHEL... The release of AlmaLinux OS 10.2 in May 2026 reveals just how far AlmaLinux has come.... When RHEL 10 increased the x86-64-v2 architecture baseline to x86-64-v3, many older server platforms (and some new ones) were left in the lurch. These older servers couldn't support the modern CPU feature sets in x86-64-v3, including AVX2 CPU instructions. AlmaLinux recognized that many community members employed older hardware that relied on x86-64-v2. items.title: Building Ping Hunt: a GPS treasure hunt app for iOS and Android
items.summary: Looking for a treasure hunt near you? Ping Hunt turns an ordinary walk into a GPS scavenger hunt — you follow waypoints to real places and match what you see against the viewfinder. I have been building Ping Hunt as a small solo mobile project, and you can find it here: https://www.pinghunt.com It is available on both platforms: iOS: Ping Hunt on the App Store Android: Ping Hunt on Google Play How it works Open the app and pick a hunt near you. Follow the GPS coordinates to each waypoint. Match the view in the camera viewfinder to unlock the next step. No setup, no library of pre-made caches to manage — you just open the app and play the hunt that is right in front of you. Modern phones already know exactly where you are and what you are looking at. The hard part was never the GPS; it was turning "you are here" into something that feels like play. So Ping Hunt removes the busywork of classic geocaching — logging finds, maintaining a profile, managing dozens of tiny icons in a map — and keeps the part that is fun: walking somewhere because there is a small mystery waiting there. Glaciers, which are still responding to historical warming, would only preserve about 70% of their current volume over a timescale of centuries if long-term heating were brought back down to 0.8C, the report found. items.title: How are you dealing with all the negative side effects of AI on the web?
items.summary: It seems to me that the AI hype killed the web for good, but not for the reasons we immediately associate with it. Search engines now rank links full of slop at the top, which ironically make LLM summaries acceptable, not because they are better than what we had before (they are not), but because they at least mention the good links which are now buried at the bottom of the page. Also, they've been rate limiting ordinary users like crazy: more often than I'd like to, Google and DuckDuckGo now either show me either an error message or tell me to wait a bit. Sometimes I waste at least a minute refreshing the page and waiting for a result. I also can't browse GitHub freely without being logged in. Anubis is now everywhere, occasionally blocking me. I feel like my productivity has actually gone down thanks to all of that. items.title: Vibrating Mattress Helps Clear Alzheimer's Protein From the Brain
items.summary: A vibrating mattress combined with two pills that release nitric oxide enhanced the brain's ability to clear an Alzheimer's-related protein. According to New Scientist, the experiment "caused the brain's blood vessels to swell and constrict more strongly, which enhanced the glymphatic system's clearance of [the protein]." From the report: [Kesa Kiviniemi at the University of Oulu in Finland] and his colleagues recruited 29 adults who hadn't been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease or any other cognitive issues. The participants took a pill that dissolves when under the tongue, releasing nitric oxide. They then lay on a mattress that caused their bodies to gently vibrate for 40 minutes, taking another pill halfway through. Blood samples revealed that their levels of a type of protein called beta-amyloid 42 increased by 35 per cent, on average, after the intervention. This protein, which usually helps neurons signal and connect to each other, misfolds and form clumps in Alzheimer's disease. items.title: How I built a Wordle-style daily puzzle in SwiftUI (no backend)
items.summary: I recently shipped Gemdoku: Daily Block Puzzle, a 9×9 block puzzle for iPhone. The core feature is a Wordle-style Daily Challenge: every player in the world gets the same goal, the same move limit and the exact same sequence of pieces each day. It turned out to be a fun little engineering problem. Here's how it works under the hood, all in plain Swift and SwiftUI, with no backend. items.title: Mining 14,351 Chess Puzzles with Stockfish 18 (and the Illegal-FEN Trap in chess.js)
items.summary: When we started building Brass Pawn (source on GitHub, AGPLv3), we needed a large offline tactics, positional judgement, and endgame dataset that ran completely on-device—both in the browser and natively on iPhone, iPad, and Mac. Transcribing chess puzzles by hand or scraping unverified problem collections breaks down fast. Two failure modes show up immediately in real training: Cooked solutions: A position has a flashy sacrifice, so a human annotator marks it as winning—missing a quiet defensive resource at depth 18, or missing a second equally winning move that punishes a student for playing an objectively strong alternative. Horizon flips: A shallow engine pass (depth 10–12) flags a move as +2.10, only for depth 22 to reveal perpetual check (0.00). Instead of transcribing puzzles, we built a deterministic mining and independent verification pipeline powered by Stockfish 18. Along the way, we hit a subtle FEN validation edge case in chess.js that silently breaks UCI engines. A good tactics puzzle isn't simply "someone blundered in a game." items.title: Making a SwiftUI app survive a folding iPhone: what broke on the iPhone Duo and how I fixed it
items.summary: I make PawLife, a small pet health app (feeding plans in grams, a health diary, a food safety lookup). It is one SwiftUI codebase for iPhone, iPad, Mac Catalyst, Apple Watch and visionOS. When Xcode 27.2 shipped simulators for the iPhone Duo, I expected "it is just a wider iPhone". It is not. Here is what actually broke, in the order I found it, and what the fixes looked like. The Duo has an outer display and an inner one across the fold. Your app runs on one of them at a time, and the window changes size when the user folds or unfolds. The simulator reports it as a window resize, not a new scene. Measured on the simulator: Folded: a 466×678 pt window, of which my app got 382 pt of width. The remaining 84 pt on the trailing edge is a reserved column (status area and camera) exposed through the safe area. Open: a landscape 951×669 pt window, 867 pt for the app, with the same 84 pt trailing column. So the app goes from a narrow portrait phone to a wide landscape slab and back, live, without a relaunch. items.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true
items.summary: Nintendo Switch 2; Nintendo This ambitious remake transforms a landmark Zelda game into a modern masterpiece, clearer and easier to navigate, more beautiful to look at, with playful musical touches. Yet the melancholy remains It’s always a worry, returning to a formative piece of art from your childhood. Will your jaded adult sensibilities render you unable to locate the magic that captivated your child self? Will revisiting it reveal that it was never actually that good, and that your tastes are built on a foundation of lies? With video games, there is the added complication of technological advancement: decades-old games can look so basic and feel so treacly to play that it’s hard to explain why they were mind-blowing at the time. Light-touch remasters aim to bring such games up to modern graphical standards without fundamentally changing them; an ambitious remake attempts to transform the work into something that can stand alongside any modern masterpiece. Ocarina of Time is the latter. And I could not be more delighted to report that it is a dream come true. Continue reading...

The old constraints of software engineering have disappeared, allowing startups to move faster, but also break things. The new constraints are too much context switching, losing shared context, tougher pacing, less focus on design, and AI plan limits. Many existing technologies and processes will crack under the change.

items.title: Progress on provable inference for large language models (30 minute read)
items.summary: It is almost impossible to verify which model produced a specific output. Cryptographic proofs of inference allow model providers to prove that preach suppose was produced which a specific model. These proofs could enable new applications and contribute to a toolkit for verifying compliance with AI pacing requirements. This post details the progress made on a powerful type of cryptographic proof uniquely fit for provable inference called zKSNARK.

items.title: Interpolative Software (5 minute read)
items.summary: Interpolative software is code that is solidly within the training distribution of models. It can often be specified with just a few sentences of prompting. Novel software is something that has fundamentally not existed before. Writing novel software with agents is challenging, as they are not trained on the task. Not a lot of software is novel, which is fine, as there is still a ton of value in the interpolative stuff.
